claim: Perilipin (PLIN) proteins constitute an ancient family important in lipid droplet (LD) formation and triglyceride metabolism.
source: Perilipin (PLIN) proteins constitute an ancient family important in lipid droplet (LD) formation and triglyceride metabolism.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific knowledge about PLIN proteins.

claim: An additional PLIN clade (plin6) is unique to teleosts.
source: We identified an additional PLIN clade (plin6) that is unique to teleosts and can be traced to the two whole genome duplications that occurred early in vertebrate evolution.
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis in Figure 1 shows plin6 is present only in teleost fish species.

claim: Plin6 can be traced to the two whole genome duplications that occurred early in vertebrate evolution.
source: We identified an additional PLIN clade (plin6) that is unique to teleosts and can be traced to the two whole genome duplications that occurred early in vertebrate evolution.
evidence: Phylogenetic and synteny analyses demonstrate the evolutionary origin of plin6 from vertebrate genome duplications.

claim: Plin6 is highly expressed in skin xanthophores.
source: Plin6 is highly expressed in skin xanthophores, which mediate red/yellow pigmentation and trafficking, but not in tissues associated with lipid metabolism.
evidence: RT-PCR and immunohistochemistry data in Figure 3 demonstrate high expression in skin and localization to xanthophores.

claim: Xanthophores mediate red/yellow pigmentation and trafficking.
source: Plin6 is highly expressed in skin xanthophores, which mediate red/yellow pigmentation and trafficking, but not in tissues associated with lipid metabolism.
evidence: This is established knowledge about xanthophore function.

claim: Plin6 is not expressed in tissues associated with lipid metabolism.
source: Plin6 is highly expressed in skin xanthophores, which mediate red/yellow pigmentation and trafficking, but not in tissues associated with lipid metabolism.
evidence: RT-PCR data in Figure 3B shows much higher expression in skin than fat, and Western blot in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 shows absence in liver and muscle.

claim: Zebrafish Plin6 protein targets the surface of pigment-containing carotenoid droplets (CD).
source: Biochemical and immunochemical analyses demonstrate that zebrafish Plin6 protein targets the surface of pigment-containing carotenoid droplets (CD).
evidence: Immunofluorescence in Figure 4 and immunoTEM in Figure 5C demonstrate Plin6 localization to CD surfaces.

claim: Protein kinase A (PKA) activation mediates CD dispersion in xanthophores.
source: Protein kinase A (PKA) activation, which mediates CD dispersion in xanthophores, phosphorylates Plin6 on conserved residues.
evidence: Figure 4 shows forskolin-IBMX (PKA activator) induces CD dispersion.

claim: PKA activation phosphorylates Plin6 on conserved residues.
source: Protein kinase A (PKA) activation, which mediates CD dispersion in xanthophores, phosphorylates Plin6 on conserved residues.
evidence: Phos-tag gel analysis in Figure 5B shows increased phosphorylation of Plin6 upon PKA activation with forskolin-IBMX.

claim: Knockout of plin6 in zebrafish severely impairs the ability of CD to concentrate carotenoids.
source: Knockout of plin6 in zebrafish severely impairs the ability of CD to concentrate carotenoids and prevents tight clustering of CD within carotenoid bodies.
evidence: Figure 6 shows plin6 mutants have reduced carotenoid pigmentation and quantification shows >50% reduction in skin carotenoid levels.

claim: Knockout of plin6 prevents tight clustering of CD within carotenoid bodies.
source: Knockout of plin6 in zebrafish severely impairs the ability of CD to concentrate carotenoids and prevents tight clustering of CD within carotenoid bodies.
evidence: Figure 7 shows plin6 mutants fail to tightly aggregate CD in response to epinephrine treatment.

claim: LD and CD are homologous structures.
source: Ultrastructural and functional analyses indicate that LD and CD are homologous structures, and that Plin6 was functionalized early in vertebrate evolution for concentrating and trafficking pigment.
evidence: Figure 8 shows zebrafish Plin6 targets mammalian lipid droplets, and ultrastructural analysis shows similar phospholipid monolayer structure.

claim: Plin6 was functionalized early in vertebrate evolution for concentrating and trafficking pigment.
source: Ultrastructural and functional analyses indicate that LD and CD are homologous structures, and that Plin6 was functionalized early in vertebrate evolution for concentrating and trafficking pigment.
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis shows plin6 originated from vertebrate genome duplications, and functional data shows its role in pigment concentration and trafficking.

claim: Intracellular structures that assimilate and traffic lipophilic cargo can be found in virtually every eukaryotic cell.
source: Intracellular structures that assimilate and traffic lipophilic cargo can be found in virtually every eukaryotic cell, including those from algae, yeast, plants, insects, and vertebrates (Zweytick et al., 2000; Arrese et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Lipid droplets typically store neutral lipids like triglyceride and cholesterol esters.
source: Perhaps best known of these structures are the intracellular lipid droplets (LD), which typically store neutral lipids like triglyceride and cholesterol esters, and play diverse roles in metabolism and signaling.
evidence: This is established knowledge about lipid droplet composition.

claim: Lipid droplets play diverse roles in metabolism and signaling.
source: Perhaps best known of these structures are the intracellular lipid droplets (LD), which typically store neutral lipids like triglyceride and cholesterol esters, and play diverse roles in metabolism and signaling.
evidence: This is established knowledge about lipid droplet function.

claim: Intracellular organelles that traffic lipophilic cargo share a simple structure: a central core of lipophilic cargo surrounded by a phospholipid monolayer that is embedded with critical proteins.
source: These intracellular organelles share a simple structure: a central core of lipophilic cargo surrounded by a phospholipid monolayer that is embedded with critical proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the structure of lipid droplets and similar organelles.

claim: Intracellular LD were once considered to be inert lipid 'inclusions'.
source: Until recently, intracellular LD were considered to be inert lipid 'inclusions'; however, growing evidence indicates that LD are bona fide organelles whose function is controlled in part by an evolutionarily-conserved protein network (Farese and Walther, 2009; Walther and Farese, 2012).
evidence: This is a historical statement about how lipid droplets were previously viewed.

claim: Growing evidence indicates that LD are bona fide organelles whose function is controlled in part by an evolutionarily-conserved protein network.
source: Until recently, intracellular LD were considered to be inert lipid 'inclusions'; however, growing evidence indicates that LD are bona fide organelles whose function is controlled in part by an evolutionarily-conserved protein network (Farese and Walther, 2009; Walther and Farese, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Perilipin (PLIN) proteins are important in the generation of LD and in regulating protein trafficking on the LD.
source: Recent work has revealed the importance of Perilipin (PLIN) proteins in the generation of LD and in regulating protein trafficking on the LD (Brasaemle et al., 2004; Londos et al., 2005; Granneman and Moore, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PLINs comprise an ancient gene family that plays central roles in neutral lipid metabolism.
source: PLINs comprise an ancient gene family that plays central roles in neutral lipid metabolism (Miura et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Mammalian PLIN proteins contain a conserved PAT domain that appears to be important in LD targeting.
source: Mammalian PLIN proteins contain a conserved PAT domain (for Perilipin, Adipophilin, TIP47; now named Plin1, Plin2 and Plin3, respectively) that appears to be important in LD targeting (Londos et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The human genome has five PLIN genes, designated PLIN1-5.
source: The human genome has five PLIN genes, designated PLIN1-5.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the human PLIN gene family.

claim: PLIN2 and PLIN3 are found in most cells and are thought to be involved in the formation and expansion of LD from the smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER).
source: PLIN2 and PLIN3 are found in most cells and are thought to be involved in the formation and expansion of LD from the smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER) (Wolins et al., 2006; Ducharme and Bickel, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Tissue-specific PLINs have evolved in mammals that confer functional diversity.
source: In addition, tissue-specific PLINs have evolved in mammals that confer functional diversity.
evidence: This is supported by the examples given in the following sentence about Plin1 and Plin5.

claim: Plin1 mediates hormone-stimulated lipolysis in fat cells.
source: For example, Plin1 mediates hormone-stimulated lipolysis in fat cells, which supply tissues with energy in the form of fatty acids, whereas Plin5 manages fatty acid storage/oxidation in muscle cells (Moore et al., 2005; Wolins et al., 2006; Granneman et al., 2011; Sanders et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Fat cells supply tissues with energy in the form of fatty acids.
source: For example, Plin1 mediates hormone-stimulated lipolysis in fat cells, which supply tissues with energy in the form of fatty acids, whereas Plin5 manages fatty acid storage/oxidation in muscle cells (Moore et al., 2005; Wolins et al., 2006; Granneman et al., 2011; Sanders et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about fat cell function.

claim: Plin5 manages fatty acid storage/oxidation in muscle cells.
source: For example, Plin1 mediates hormone-stimulated lipolysis in fat cells, which supply tissues with energy in the form of fatty acids, whereas Plin5 manages fatty acid storage/oxidation in muscle cells (Moore et al., 2005; Wolins et al., 2006; Granneman et al., 2011; Sanders et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Most work addressing PLIN protein function has been performed in mammalian systems, focusing on neutral lipid metabolism.
source: Most work addressing PLIN protein function has been performed in mammalian systems, focusing on neutral lipid metabolism, but relatively little has been performed on non-mammalian vertebrates.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field.

claim: Relatively little work on PLIN protein function has been performed on non-mammalian vertebrates.
source: Most work addressing PLIN protein function has been performed in mammalian systems, focusing on neutral lipid metabolism, but relatively little has been performed on non-mammalian vertebrates.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field.

claim: Database analysis identified a novel PLIN clade (plin6) that has existed in vertebrates since before the divergence of the fish and human lineages.
source: Our database analysis identified a novel PLIN clade (plin6) that has existed in vertebrates since before the divergence of the fish and human lineages.
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis in Figure 1 and synteny analysis in Figure 2 support this conclusion.

claim: Plin6 is targeted to intracellular carotenoid droplets.
source: Structural and functional analyses indicate that Plin6 is targeted to intracellular carotenoid droplets, where it plays a role in concentrating and trafficking lipophilic pigments.
evidence: Immunofluorescence and immunoTEM data in Figures 4 and 5 demonstrate Plin6 localization to carotenoid droplets.

claim: Plin6 plays a role in concentrating and trafficking lipophilic pigments.
source: Structural and functional analyses indicate that Plin6 is targeted to intracellular carotenoid droplets, where it plays a role in concentrating and trafficking lipophilic pigments.
evidence: Knockout data in Figures 6 and 7 show reduced carotenoid concentration and impaired aggregation in plin6 mutants.

claim: Database analysis identified four zebrafish plin paralogs.
source: Our database analysis identified four zebrafish plin paralogs.
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis in Figure 1 shows four zebrafish plin genes.

claim: The three human genes PLIN1, PLIN2, and PLIN3 each have clear zebrafish orthologs: plin1, plin2 and plin3.
source: Phylogenetic and conserved synteny analysis indicated that the three human genes PLIN1, PLIN2, and PLIN3 each have clear zebrafish orthologs: plin1 (XP_003200505.1), plin2 (NP_001025433.1) and plin3 (AAH56585.1), respectively.
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis in Figure 1 demonstrates orthology relationships.

claim: The fourth zebrafish paralog (NP_001103951.1) is currently annotated as a 'hypothetical protein (zgc:162150, ENSDARG00000076844.4)'.
source: The fourth zebrafish paralog (NP_001103951.1), currently annotated as a 'hypothetical protein (zgc:162150, ENSDARG00000076844.4),' was restricted to a phyologenetic clade that is distinct from the other PLIN genes (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a statement about the current annotation of the gene.

claim: The fourth zebrafish paralog was restricted to a phylogenetic clade that is distinct from the other PLIN genes.
source: The fourth zebrafish paralog (NP_001103951.1), currently annotated as a 'hypothetical protein (zgc:162150, ENSDARG00000076844.4),' was restricted to a phyologenetic clade that is distinct from the other PLIN genes (Figure 1).
evidence: Figure 1 shows the phylogenetic tree with plin6 forming a distinct clade.

claim: Orthologs of plin6 were identified only in ray fin fish (actinopterygians).
source: Orthologs of plin6 were identified only in ray fin fish (actinopterygians), including zebrafish (Danio rerio), pufferfish (Tetraodon nigroviridis; CAF95167.1 and Takifugu rubripes; XP_003965836.1), tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus; XP_003451283.1) and medaka (Oryzias latipes; XP_004078586.1).
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis in Figure 1 shows plin6 orthologs only in ray fin fish.

claim: A plin6 ortholog is present in the spotted gar.
source: Importantly, a plin6 ortholog is present in the spotted gar (Braasch et al., 2016), which diverged from the teleost lineage prior to the teleost genome duplication (TGD) about 350 Mya (Amores et al., 2011), suggesting an ancient origin of this clade.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and phylogenetic analysis in Figure 1.

claim: Spotted gar diverged from the teleost lineage prior to the teleost genome duplication (TGD) about 350 Mya.
source: Importantly, a plin6 ortholog is present in the spotted gar (Braasch et al., 2016), which diverged from the teleost lineage prior to the teleost genome duplication (TGD) about 350 Mya (Amores et al., 2011), suggesting an ancient origin of this clade.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The presence of plin6 in spotted gar suggests an ancient origin of this clade.
source: Importantly, a plin6 ortholog is present in the spotted gar (Braasch et al., 2016), which diverged from the teleost lineage prior to the teleost genome duplication (TGD) about 350 Mya (Amores et al., 2011), suggesting an ancient origin of this clade.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic distribution of plin6.

claim: All existing vertebrate PLIN genes can be traced to one of the four products resulting from two genome duplication events that occurred in early vertebrate evolution (VGD1 and VGD2).
source: Finally, as we detail below, systematic phylogenetic and conserved synteny analyses revealed that all existing vertebrate PLIN genes can be traced to one of the four products resulting from two genome duplication events that occurred in early vertebrate evolution (VGD1 and VGD2) (Holland, 1999; Dehal and Boore, 2005; Nakatani et al., 2007; Cañestro et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic and synteny analyses in Figures 1 and 2, and citations to previous literature.

claim: The last common ancestor of all bony fish had a plin1 gene.
source: We conclude that the last common ancestor of all bony fish had a plin1 gene.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution of plin1 orthologs shown in Figure 1.

claim: PLIN2 orthologs can be identified in tetrapods, coelacanth, numerous teleost species, and spotted gar.
source: Phylogenetic analysis identified PLIN2 orthologs in tetrapods, in coelacanth, in numerous teleost species, as well as in spotted gar (Figure 1).
evidence: Figure 1 shows the phylogenetic distribution of PLIN2 orthologs.

claim: Stickleback, Amazon molly, and some other percomorphs retained two copies of plin2 that arose in the teleost genome duplication.
source: This analysis shows that stickleback, Amazon molly, and some other percomorphs retained two copies of plin2 that arose in the teleost genome duplication (Amores et al., 1998; Postlethwait et al., 1999; Taylor et al., 2003; Jaillon et al., 2004b); we call these genes plin2a (e.g., ENSGACG00000019638) and plin2b (e.g., ENSGACG00000017870).
evidence: This is supported by conserved synteny analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citations.

claim: In the human genome, PLIN4, PLIN5, and PLIN3 reside in a 15-gene interval.
source: In the human genome, PLIN4, PLIN5, and PLIN3, reside in a 15-gene interval, suggesting an origin by tandem duplication (Figure 2A).
evidence: Figure 2A shows the genomic location of these genes.

claim: The location of PLIN4, PLIN5, and PLIN3 in a 15-gene interval suggests an origin by tandem duplication.
source: In the human genome, PLIN4, PLIN5, and PLIN3, reside in a 15-gene interval, suggesting an origin by tandem duplication (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the genomic organization of these genes.

claim: Coelacanth has a single gene equally related phylogenetically to human PLIN3 and PLIN5.
source: Furthermore, coelacanth, a basally diverging lobefin vertebrate, has a single gene (ENSLACG00000013515) equally related phylogenetically to human PLIN3 and PLIN5 (Figure 1).
evidence: Figure 1 shows the phylogenetic relationship of the coelacanth gene to PLIN3 and PLIN5.

claim: Rayfin fish have a single gene that is phylogenetically equally related to the amniote PLIN3 and PLIN5.
source: Rayfin fish, including teleosts and spotted gar, a basally diverging rayfin, have a single gene that is phylogenetically equally related to the amniote PLIN3 and PLIN5 (Figure 1).
evidence: Figure 1 shows the phylogenetic relationship of rayfin fish genes to PLIN3 and PLIN5.

claim: The human chromosome segment containing PLIN4, PLIN5, and PLIN3 on Hsa19 is orthologous to the region of Dre8 that contains the zebrafish plin5 gene.
source: The human chromosome segment containing PLIN4, PLIN5, and PLIN3 on Homo sapiens chromosome-19 (Hsa19, Figure 2A–1) is orthologous to the region of Danio rerio chromosome-8 (Dre8, Figure 2A–2) that contains the zebrafish plin5 gene (Figure 2A).
evidence: Figure 2A shows the conserved synteny between human and zebrafish chromosomes.

claim: The presence of a single plin3/4/5 gene in teleosts indicates that PLIN3/4/5 originated before the divergence of rayfin and lobefin vertebrates.
source: The presence of a single plin3/4/5 gene in teleosts (called plin5 in zebrafish) indicates that PLIN3/4/5 also originated before the divergence of rayfin and lobefin vertebrates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic distribution of plin3/4/5 genes.

claim: The adjacent or near adjacent location of PLIN4, PLIN5, and PLIN3 in the human genome suggests an origin by tandem duplication events in the tetrapod lineage after the divergence of coelacanth and human lineages.
source: And the adjacent or near adjacent location of PLIN4, PLIN5, and PLIN3 in the human genome suggests and origin by tandem duplication events in the tetrapod lineage after the divergence of coelacanth and human lineages.
evidence: This is an inference based on genomic organization and phylogenetic distribution.

claim: Birds and a lizard have a copy of PLIN3 and PLIN5.
source: Because birds and a lizard have a copy of PLIN3 and PLIN5, but PLIN4 is present only in mammals (Figure 1), we conclude that a PLIN3/4/5 gene was present in the last common ancestor of tetrapods and was duplicated in stem tetrapods to provide PLIN3 and PLIN4/5, followed by the duplication of PLIN4/5 to form the adjacent genes PLIN4 and PLIN5 in the human lineage after the divergence of mammals from reptiles (including birds).
evidence: Figure 1 shows the phylogenetic distribution of PLIN3, PLIN4, and PLIN5.

claim: PLIN4 is present only in mammals.
source: Because birds and a lizard have a copy of PLIN3 and PLIN5, but PLIN4 is present only in mammals (Figure 1), we conclude that a PLIN3/4/5 gene was present in the last common ancestor of tetrapods and was duplicated in stem tetrapods to provide PLIN3 and PLIN4/5, followed by the duplication of PLIN4/5 to form the adjacent genes PLIN4 and PLIN5 in the human lineage after the divergence of mammals from reptiles (including birds).
evidence: Figure 1 shows PLIN4 is present only in mammals.

claim: A PLIN3/4/5 gene was present in the last common ancestor of tetrapods.
source: Because birds and a lizard have a copy of PLIN3 and PLIN5, but PLIN4 is present only in mammals (Figure 1), we conclude that a PLIN3/4/5 gene was present in the last common ancestor of tetrapods and was duplicated in stem tetrapods to provide PLIN3 and PLIN4/5, followed by the duplication of PLIN4/5 to form the adjacent genes PLIN4 and PLIN5 in the human lineage after the divergence of mammals from reptiles (including birds).
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution of PLIN3/4/5 genes.

claim: PLIN3/4/5 was duplicated in stem tetrapods to provide PLIN3 and PLIN4/5.
source: Because birds and a lizard have a copy of PLIN3 and PLIN5, but PLIN4 is present only in mammals (Figure 1), we conclude that a PLIN3/4/5 gene was present in the last common ancestor of tetrapods and was duplicated in stem tetrapods to provide PLIN3 and PLIN4/5, followed by the duplication of PLIN4/5 to form the adjacent genes PLIN4 and PLIN5 in the human lineage after the divergence of mammals from reptiles (including birds).
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution of PLIN3/4/5 genes.

claim: PLIN4/5 was duplicated to form the adjacent genes PLIN4 and PLIN5 in the human lineage after the divergence of mammals from reptiles.
source: Because birds and a lizard have a copy of PLIN3 and PLIN5, but PLIN4 is present only in mammals (Figure 1), we conclude that a PLIN3/4/5 gene was present in the last common ancestor of tetrapods and was duplicated in stem tetrapods to provide PLIN3 and PLIN4/5, followed by the duplication of PLIN4/5 to form the adjacent genes PLIN4 and PLIN5 in the human lineage after the divergence of mammals from reptiles (including birds).
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution and genomic organization of PLIN4 and PLIN5.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis of PLIN-family genes identified a rayfin plin clade that includes spotted gar and two major teleost clades but excludes lobe fin species.
source: Phylogenetic analysis of PLIN-family genes identified a rayfin plin clade that includes spotted gar and two major teleost clades: ostariophysans, including zebrafish and Astyanax cavefish; and percomorphs, including the pufferfish Tetraodon nigroviridis, Amazon molly, and tilapia, but excludes lobe fin species (Figure 1).
evidence: Figure 1 shows the phylogenetic tree with plin6 present only in rayfin fish.

claim: Tetrapods do not appear to contain orthologs of plin6.
source: Here we rename this PLIN-related gene as plin6. Tetrapods do not appear to contain orthologs of plin6 (Figure 1).
evidence: Figure 1 shows plin6 is absent in tetrapods.

claim: In zebrafish, plin6 lies on chromosome Dre16 at nucleotide position 28,863,080.
source: In zebrafish, plin6 lies on chromosome Dre16 at nucleotide position 28,863,080 (Figure 2B–1).
evidence: Figure 2B shows the chromosomal location of plin6 in zebrafish.

claim: The portion of zebrafish Dre16 containing plin6 shares conserved syntenies with a portion of gar linkage group Loc24 that includes the gar ortholog of plin6.
source: This portion of Dre16 shares conserved syntenies with a portion of gar linkage group Loc24 that includes the gar ortholog of plin6 (Figure 2B–2).
evidence: Figure 2B shows conserved synteny between zebrafish and gar.

claim: The portion of the gar genome containing plin6 is orthologous to a region on human chromosome Hsa1.
source: In turn, this portion of the gar genome is orthologous to a region on human chromosome Hsa1 (Figures 2B–3).
evidence: Figure 2B shows conserved synteny between gar and human.

claim: Chromosome rearrangements in the lobefin lineage likely led to the destruction of the plin6 ortholog.
source: This result indicates that chromosome rearrangements in the lobefin lineage likely led to the destruction of the plin6 ortholog.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of plin6 in the expected location in the human genome despite conserved synteny.

claim: The chromosome region containing plin6 was retained in the ray fin and human lineages.
source: We conclude that the chromosome region containing plin6 was retained in the ray fin and human lineages but that plin6 appears only in the ray fin lineage, a result compatible with the VGD2-origin hypothesis or the retrotransposition hypothesis but not the tandem duplication mechanism for origin of plin6.
evidence: This is inferred from conserved synteny analysis.

claim: Plin6 appears only in the ray fin lineage.
source: We conclude that the chromosome region containing plin6 was retained in the ray fin and human lineages but that plin6 appears only in the ray fin lineage, a result compatible with the VGD2-origin hypothesis or the retrotransposition hypothesis but not the tandem duplication mechanism for origin of plin6.
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis in Figure 1 shows plin6 is present only in ray fin fish.

claim: The distribution of plin6 is compatible with the VGD2-origin hypothesis or the retrotransposition hypothesis but not the tandem duplication mechanism.
source: We conclude that the chromosome region containing plin6 was retained in the ray fin and human lineages but that plin6 appears only in the ray fin lineage, a result compatible with the VGD2-origin hypothesis or the retrotransposition hypothesis but not the tandem duplication mechanism for origin of plin6.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution and synteny analysis.

claim: The region of Hsa1 that is predicted to be orthologous to the plin6-containing region of zebrafish and gar is in the portion of Hsa1 predicted to be paralogous to the regions of Hsa9, Hsa15, and Hsa19 that contain the PLIN2, PLIN1, and PLIN4-PLIN5-PLIN3 loci, respectively.
source: The region of Hsa1 that is predicted to be orthologous to the plin6-containing region of zebrafish and gar (Figures 2B–3) is in the portion of Hsa1 predicted to be paralogous to the regions of Hsa9, Hsa15, and Hsa19 that contain the PLIN2, PLIN1, and PLIN4-PLIN5-PLIN3 loci, respectively (Figure 2C).
evidence: Figure 2C shows the paralogous relationships between human chromosomes.

claim: Portions of human chromosomes Hsa1, Hsa9, Hsa15, and Hsa19 were previously shown to be derived from the VGD1 and VGD2 events.
source: These portions of human chromosomes Hsa1, Hsa9, Hsa15, and Hsa19 were previously shown to be derived from the VGD1 and VGD2 events (Dehal and Boore, 2005; Nakatani et al., 2007; Cañestro et al., 2009) as predicted by the hypothesis that plin6 originated in the second round of vertebrate genome duplication.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Plin6 is an ohnolog derived from the VGD1 and VGD2 events that has gone missing in the lobefin lineage.
source: Therefore, we conclude that plin6 is an ohnolog derived from the VGD1 and VGD2 events that has gone missing in the lobefin lineage.
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic and synteny analyses showing plin6 is paralogous to other PLIN genes and absent in lobefins.

claim: Zebrafish plin6 mRNA encodes a 490 amino acid residue protein.
source: Zebrafish plin6 mRNA encodes a 490 amino acid residue protein that contains an N-terminal PAT domain (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and three consensus sites for protein kinase A (PKA) phosphorylation in the C-terminal region (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the conceptual translation of the plin6 mRNA sequence.

claim: Zebrafish Plin6 contains an N-terminal PAT domain.
source: Zebrafish plin6 mRNA encodes a 490 amino acid residue protein that contains an N-terminal PAT domain (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and three consensus sites for protein kinase A (PKA) phosphorylation in the C-terminal region (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1 shows the PAT domain in the protein sequence alignment.

claim: Zebrafish Plin6 contains three consensus sites for protein kinase A (PKA) phosphorylation in the C-terminal region.
source: Zebrafish plin6 mRNA encodes a 490 amino acid residue protein that contains an N-terminal PAT domain (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and three consensus sites for protein kinase A (PKA) phosphorylation in the C-terminal region (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1 shows the PKA sites in the protein sequence alignment.

claim: The overall sequence similarity of Plin6 with the other zebrafish Plin paralogs ranged from 29–34%.
source: The overall sequence similarity of Plin6 with the other zebrafish Plin paralogs ranged from 29–34%, and was largely limited to the conserved N-terminal PAT domain (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2.

claim: The sequence similarity of Plin6 with other zebrafish Plin paralogs was largely limited to the conserved N-terminal PAT domain.
source: The overall sequence similarity of Plin6 with the other zebrafish Plin paralogs ranged from 29–34%, and was largely limited to the conserved N-terminal PAT domain (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2 show sequence alignments with conservation primarily in the PAT domain.

claim: The three PKA sites in the C-terminus of zebrafish Plin6 were conserved in pufferfish, tilapia, medaka, and goldfish.
source: Importantly, the three PKA sites that were found in the C-terminus of zebrafish Plin6 were conserved in pufferfish, tilapia, medaka, goldfish (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), with the final PKA site conserved in spotted gar (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), strongly indicating that they are ancient and functionally significant.
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 3 shows conservation of PKA sites across species.

claim: The final PKA site in Plin6 is conserved in spotted gar.
source: Importantly, the three PKA sites that were found in the C-terminus of zebrafish Plin6 were conserved in pufferfish, tilapia, medaka, goldfish (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), with the final PKA site conserved in spotted gar (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), strongly indicating that they are ancient and functionally significant.
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 3 shows conservation of the final PKA site in spotted gar.

claim: The conservation of PKA sites in Plin6 across species strongly indicates that they are ancient and functionally significant.
source: Importantly, the three PKA sites that were found in the C-terminus of zebrafish Plin6 were conserved in pufferfish, tilapia, medaka, goldfish (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), with the final PKA site conserved in spotted gar (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), strongly indicating that they are ancient and functionally significant.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic conservation of the PKA sites.

claim: During early development, expression of plin6 was strong in 3 days post-fertilization (dpf) embryos and continued at least into larval stages.
source: During early development, expression of plin6 was strong in 3 days post-fertilization (dpf) embryos and continued at least into larval stages (Figure 3A).
evidence: Figure 3A shows RT-PCR results demonstrating plin6 expression at various developmental stages.

claim: In the adult, real-time PCR showed abundant expression of plin6 in skin.
source: In the adult, contrary to the expectation that plin6 would be expressed in fat cells, real-time PCR showed abundant expression of plin6 in skin, where we detected plin6 expression levels to be 37-fold higher than that observed in adipose tissue (Figure 3B).
evidence: Figure 3B shows quantitative RT-PCR results comparing plin6 expression in skin and fat.

claim: Plin6 expression levels in skin are 37-fold higher than in adipose tissue.
source: In the adult, contrary to the expectation that plin6 would be expressed in fat cells, real-time PCR showed abundant expression of plin6 in skin, where we detected plin6 expression levels to be 37-fold higher than that observed in adipose tissue (Figure 3B).
evidence: Figure 3B shows quantitative RT-PCR results with 37-fold difference.

claim: Plin6 immunolocalized to the integumentum in 72 hr post-fertilization (hpf) embryos.
source: We confirmed that Plin6 immunolocalized to the integumentum in 72 hr post-fertilization (hpf) embryos (Figure 3C–1), in histological sections of adult skin (Figure 3C–2) and scales (Figure 3C–3), and that Plin6 was not expressed in adult muscle, liver, or gut tissue (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 3C-1 shows immunofluorescence of Plin6 in embryo integument.

claim: Plin6 immunolocalized to histological sections of adult skin.
source: We confirmed that Plin6 immunolocalized to the integumentum in 72 hr post-fertilization (hpf) embryos (Figure 3C–1), in histological sections of adult skin (Figure 3C–2) and scales (Figure 3C–3), and that Plin6 was not expressed in adult muscle, liver, or gut tissue (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 3C-2 shows immunofluorescence of Plin6 in adult skin sections.

claim: Plin6 immunolocalized to adult scales.
source: We confirmed that Plin6 immunolocalized to the integumentum in 72 hr post-fertilization (hpf) embryos (Figure 3C–1), in histological sections of adult skin (Figure 3C–2) and scales (Figure 3C–3), and that Plin6 was not expressed in adult muscle, liver, or gut tissue (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 3C-3 shows immunofluorescence of Plin6 in adult scales.

claim: Plin6 was not expressed in adult muscle, liver, or gut tissue.
source: We confirmed that Plin6 immunolocalized to the integumentum in 72 hr post-fertilization (hpf) embryos (Figure 3C–1), in histological sections of adult skin (Figure 3C–2) and scales (Figure 3C–3), and that Plin6 was not expressed in adult muscle, liver, or gut tissue (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1 shows Western blot with no Plin6 expression in muscle, liver, or gut.

claim: The stellate morphology of Plin6 expression in adult scales is consistent with immunolocalization to xanthophores.
source: The stellate morphology of the position of the protein in adult scales is consistent with Plin6 immunolocalization to xanthophores, which we later more definitively confirmed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the morphology observed in Figure 3C-3.

claim: Xanthophores are chromatophores that concentrate yellow/orange pigment in poikilothermic vertebrates such as amphibians, reptiles, and fish, but not birds or mammals.
source: Xanthophores are chromatophores that concentrate yellow/orange pigment in poikilothermic vertebrates such as amphibians, reptiles, and fish, but not birds or mammals (Kimura et al., 2014; Parichy and Spiewak, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In teleost fish, xanthophores contain yellow pteridine pigments stored in pterinosomes.
source: In teleost fish, xanthophores contain yellow pteridine pigments stored in pterinosomes (Matsumoto, 1965; Matsumoto and Obika, 1968; Khoo and Phang, 1992, 2012), and red/orange carotenoid pigments stored in carotenoid droplets (Goodrich et al., 1941; Matsumoto, 1965).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In teleost fish, xanthophores contain red/orange carotenoid pigments stored in carotenoid droplets.
source: In teleost fish, xanthophores contain yellow pteridine pigments stored in pterinosomes (Matsumoto, 1965; Matsumoto and Obika, 1968; Khoo and Phang, 1992, 2012), and red/orange carotenoid pigments stored in carotenoid droplets (Goodrich et al., 1941; Matsumoto, 1965).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pterinosomes and CD can be readily distinguished by numerous criteria.
source: Pterinosomes and CD can be readily distinguished by numerous criteria; for example, CD possesses hydrophobic carotenoids that disperse from a perinuclear aggregate in response to PKA activation and fluoresce when excited by blue light (Goodrich et al., 1941; Matsumoto, 1965; Bagnara and Hadley, 1969; Lynch et al., 1986a, 1986b; Khoo and Phang, 1992; Kimler et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CD possesses hydrophobic carotenoids that disperse from a perinuclear aggregate in response to PKA activation.
source: Pterinosomes and CD can be readily distinguished by numerous criteria; for example, CD possesses hydrophobic carotenoids that disperse from a perinuclear aggregate in response to PKA activation and fluoresce when excited by blue light (Goodrich et al., 1941; Matsumoto, 1965; Bagnara and Hadley, 1969; Lynch et al., 1986a, 1986b; Khoo and Phang, 1992; Kimler et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and demonstrated in Figure 4.

claim: CD fluoresce when excited by blue light.
source: Pterinosomes and CD can be readily distinguished by numerous criteria; for example, CD possesses hydrophobic carotenoids that disperse from a perinuclear aggregate in response to PKA activation and fluoresce when excited by blue light (Goodrich et al., 1941; Matsumoto, 1965; Bagnara and Hadley, 1969; Lynch et al., 1986a, 1986b; Khoo and Phang, 1992; Kimler et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and demonstrated in Figure 4.

claim: A dense aggregation of CD was observed in the perinuclear region of zebrafish xanthophores under basal conditions.
source: We observed a dense aggregation of CD in the perinuclear region of zebrafish xanthophores under basal conditions (Figure 4B), as found in goldfish xanthophores (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), which have served as a model system for analysis of pigment trafficking (Lynch et al., 1986a, 1986b; Kimler et al., 1993).
evidence: Figure 4B shows aggregated CD in zebrafish xanthophores.

claim: Goldfish xanthophores have served as a model system for analysis of pigment trafficking.
source: We observed a dense aggregation of CD in the perinuclear region of zebrafish xanthophores under basal conditions (Figure 4B), as found in goldfish xanthophores (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), which have served as a model system for analysis of pigment trafficking (Lynch et al., 1986a, 1986b; Kimler et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CD aggregates were fluorescent when excited by blue light.
source: As expected for CDs, these aggregates were fluorescent when excited by blue light (Figure 4A', B'), and rapidly dispersed following activation of PKA with forskolin/IBMX (Figure 4C,C').
evidence: Figure 4A' and B' show fluorescence of CD aggregates.

claim: CD aggregates rapidly dispersed following activation of PKA with forskolin/IBMX.
source: As expected for CDs, these aggregates were fluorescent when excited by blue light (Figure 4A', B'), and rapidly dispersed following activation of PKA with forskolin/IBMX (Figure 4C,C').
evidence: Figure 4C and C' show dispersed CD after forskolin/IBMX treatment.

claim: Plin6 was targeted to the perinuclear region in zebrafish xanthophores under basal conditions or following treatment with epinephrine.
source: Parallel analysis of Plin6 immunolocalization in both zebrafish and goldfish xanthophores demonstrated that Plin6 was targeted to the perinuclear region under basal conditions or following treatment with epinephrine, which inhibits PKA activation (Figure 4D,G).
evidence: Figure 4D and G show Plin6 immunofluorescence in aggregated state.

claim: Epinephrine inhibits PKA activation.
source: Parallel analysis of Plin6 immunolocalization in both zebrafish and goldfish xanthophores demonstrated that Plin6 was targeted to the perinuclear region under basal conditions or following treatment with epinephrine, which inhibits PKA activation (Figure 4D,G).
evidence: This is established knowledge about epinephrine's effect on PKA.

claim: Activation of PKA with forskolin-IBMX led to rapid and extensive dispersion of Plin6 immunofluorescence throughout the xanthophore soma in both zebrafish and goldfish.
source: In contrast, activation of PKA with forskolin-IBMX led to rapid and extensive dispersion of Plin6 immunofluoresence throughout the xanthophore soma in both species (Figure 4E,H).
evidence: Figure 4E and H show dispersed Plin6 immunofluorescence after forskolin-IBMX treatment.

claim: Forskolin-IBMX treatment dramatically and significantly increased the dispersion of CD and Plin6 immunofluorescence in both zebrafish and goldfish (p<0.0001).
source: Evaluation of aggregation and dispersion in xanthophores using the semiquantitative Pigmentary Organelle Index (Taylor et al., 1991) demonstrated that forskolin-IBMX treatment dramatically and significantly increased the dispersion of CD and Plin6 immunofluorescence in both species (p<0.0001; Figure 4F,I).
evidence: Figure 4F and I show quantification of pigment dispersion with statistical significance.

claim: Plin6 immunoreactivity was highly enriched in the orange pigmented floating fraction from purified CD.
source: We purified CD by flotation of skin homogenates through a sucrose cushion and found that Plin6 immunoreactivity was highly enriched the orange pigmented floating fraction (Figure 5A).
evidence: Figure 5A shows Western blot with Plin6 enriched in the CD fraction.

claim: Immunoblotting of the CD fraction with anti-Plin6 identified a major band of 54.5 kDa.
source: Immunoblotting of the CD fraction with anti-Plin6 identified a major band of 54.5 kDa, predicted by the conceptual translation of plin6 mRNA.
evidence: Figure 5A shows a band at approximately 55 kDa in the CD fraction.

claim: The 54.5 kDa band is predicted by the conceptual translation of plin6 mRNA.
source: Immunoblotting of the CD fraction with anti-Plin6 identified a major band of 54.5 kDa, predicted by the conceptual translation of plin6 mRNA.
evidence: This is based on the predicted molecular weight from the amino acid sequence.

claim: A 39.4 kDa band appears to be a proteolytic fragment of Plin6.
source: We also observed variable levels of a 39.4 kDa band that appears to be a proteolytic fragment because its abundance increased with prolonged incubation (not shown).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the band increases with prolonged incubation.

claim: Plin6 is largely unphosphorylated under conditions that promote aggregation (epinephrine treatment).
source: Plin6 is largely unphosphorylated (Unphos, white arrowheads) under conditions that promote aggregation (Epi) and highly phosphorylated (Phos, grey arrowheads) under conditions that promote dispersion (FSK).
evidence: Figure 5B shows Phos-tag gel with unphosphorylated Plin6 after epinephrine treatment.

claim: Plin6 is highly phosphorylated under conditions that promote dispersion (forskolin-IBMX treatment).
source: Plin6 is largely unphosphorylated (Unphos, white arrowheads) under conditions that promote aggregation (Epi) and highly phosphorylated (Phos, grey arrowheads) under conditions that promote dispersion (FSK).
evidence: Figure 5B shows Phos-tag gel with phosphorylated Plin6 after forskolin-IBMX treatment.

claim: Activation of PKA by forskolin-IBMX strongly shifted most of the full length Plin6 to a low mobility band, indicating a maximally-phosphorylated state.
source: Activation of PKA by forskolin-IBMX, which promotes CD dispersion, strongly shifted most of the full length Plin6 to a low mobility band, indicating a maximally-phosphorylated state (Figure 5B).
evidence: Figure 5B shows Phos-tag gel with shifted Plin6 band after forskolin-IBMX treatment.

claim: The trafficking of Plin6 corresponds closely with that of CD.
source: The above data indicate that the trafficking of Plin6 corresponds closely with that of CD, suggesting that Plin6 might be specifically targeted to these structures.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-localization and co-trafficking data in Figure 4.

claim: Previous analysis of goldfish xanthophores indicated that CD are ~50 nm in diameter.
source: Previous analysis of goldfish xanthophores indicated that CD are ~50 nm in diameter (Kimler et al., 1993), which is too small to resolve by optical microscopy.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: CD are too small (~50 nm) to resolve by optical microscopy.
source: Previous analysis of goldfish xanthophores indicated that CD are ~50 nm in diameter (Kimler et al., 1993), which is too small to resolve by optical microscopy.
evidence: This is based on the size of CD relative to the resolution limit of optical microscopy.

claim: Zebrafish CDs are ~25 nm in diameter in both the aggregated and dispersed states.
source: Thin-section TEM of zebrafish scales indicated that zebrafish CDs are ~25 nm in diameter in both the aggregated and dispersed states (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1 shows TEM images of CD with size measurements.

claim: ImmunoTEM analysis of zebrafish skin xanthophores demonstrated that Plin6 is heavily targeted to the surface of individual CD.
source: Importantly, immunoTEM analysis of zebrafish skin xanthphores demonstrated that Plin6 is heavily targeted to the surface of individual CD and form characteristic knob-like substructures on the larger carotenoid body (Figure 5C).
evidence: Figure 5C shows immunoTEM with Plin6 localized to CD surfaces.

claim: Plin6 forms characteristic knob-like substructures on the larger carotenoid body.
source: Importantly, immunoTEM analysis of zebrafish skin xanthphores demonstrated that Plin6 is heavily targeted to the surface of individual CD and form characteristic knob-like substructures on the larger carotenoid body (Figure 5C).
evidence: Figure 5C shows immunoTEM with knob-like structures on carotenoid bodies.

claim: A stable line of plin6 knockout fish was generated using TALENs.
source: To identify the function of Plin6, we generated a stable line of plin6 knockout fish using TALENs.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used.

claim: Western blot and immunohistochemical analysis confirmed the absence of Plin6 protein in the mutant animals.
source: Western blot and immunohistochemical analysis confirmed the absence of Plin6 protein in the mutant animals (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 6—figure supplement 1 shows absence of Plin6 in knockout animals.

claim: Knockout of plin6 resulted in no apparent systemic defects in mutant embryos, larvae, or adults.
source: Knockout of plin6 resulted in no apparent systemic defects in mutant embryos, larvae, or adults and had no obvious effect on the development and location of xanthophores in the body stripes or scales (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Figure 6—figure supplement 2 shows normal development in plin6 mutants.

claim: Knockout of plin6 had no obvious effect on the development and location of xanthophores in the body stripes or scales.
source: Knockout of plin6 resulted in no apparent systemic defects in mutant embryos, larvae, or adults and had no obvious effect on the development and location of xanthophores in the body stripes or scales (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Figure 6—figure supplement 2 shows normal xanthophore distribution in plin6 mutants.

claim: Plin6 mutants exhibited a striking reduction in the amount of carotenoid pigment within the xanthophores.
source: However, plin6 mutants exhibited a striking reduction in the amount of carotenoid pigment within the xanthophores (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: Figure 6A-D shows reduced yellow pigmentation in plin6 mutants.

claim: Knockout of plin6 reduced skin carotenoid levels by more than 50% (p<0.001).
source: Analysis of carotenoid levels from whole skin extracts confirmed that knockout of plin6 reduced skin carotenoid levels by more than 50% (Figure 6E,F, p<0.001).
evidence: Figure 6E and F show quantification of carotenoid levels with >50% reduction in mutants.

claim: Knockout of plin6 reduced integumentary TAG levels by nearly 40% (p<0.02).
source: In addition, knockout of plin6 reduced integumentary TAG levels by nearly 40% (Figure 6G, p<0.02).
evidence: Figure 6G shows quantification of TAG levels with nearly 40% reduction in mutants.

claim: Plin6 mutants were unable to tightly aggregate CD within xanthophore cells in response to inhibition of PKA with epinephrine.
source: Examination of the residual carotenoid fluorescence in isolated scales (by increasing camera exposure time) indicated that plin6 mutants were unable to tightly aggregate CD within xanthophore cells in response to inhibition of PKA with epinephrine (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: Figure 7B and C show impaired CD aggregation in plin6 mutants after epinephrine treatment.

claim: Knockout of plin6 did not affect dispersion of CD into cytoplasmic processes following PKA activation by forskolin/IBMX.
source: Surprisingly, knockout of plin6 did not affect dispersion of CD into cytoplasmic processes following PKA activation by forskolin/IBMX (Figure 7B').
evidence: Figure 7B' shows normal CD dispersion in plin6 mutants after forskolin/IBMX treatment.

claim: Plin6 is required for CD aggregation, but not full CD dispersion from an already relaxed state.
source: These data show that Plin6 is required for CD aggregation, but not full CD dispersion from an already relaxed state.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of plin6 knockout on aggregation versus dispersion shown in Figure 7.

claim: Zebrafish Plin6 accumulated on the surface of LD labeled with LipidTOX when expressed alone in lipid-loaded COS7 cells.
source: We found that zebrafish Plin6 (Figure 8A,C) accumulated on the surface of LD labeled with LipidTOX when expressed alone (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: Figure 8A-C shows co-localization of EYFP-Plin6 with LipidTOX-stained lipid droplets.

claim: When Plin6 was expressed in mammalian COS7 cells, it was strongly targeted to LD containing mouse PLIN1.
source: Moreover, when Plin6 was expressed in mammalian COS7 cells, it was strongly targeted to LD containing mouse PLIN1 (Figure 8D–F), indicating that CD and LD are homologous structures.
evidence: Figure 8D-F shows co-localization of zebrafish EYFP-Plin6 with mouse Plin1-ECFP on lipid droplets.

claim: The targeting of zebrafish Plin6 to mammalian LD indicates that CD and LD are homologous structures.
source: Moreover, when Plin6 was expressed in mammalian COS7 cells, it was strongly targeted to LD containing mouse PLIN1 (Figure 8D–F), indicating that CD and LD are homologous structures.
evidence: This is inferred from the ability of Plin6 to target mammalian lipid droplets.

claim: PLINs comprise an evolutionarily conserved superfamily that plays a key role in cell-specific functions of LD.
source: PLINs comprise an evolutionarily conserved superfamily that plays a key role in cell-specific functions of LD (Miura et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The vertebrate PLIN gene family arose by the duplication of a single gene present in a chordate ancestor in two rounds of whole genome duplication at the base of the vertebrate radiation giving four genes: PLIN1, PLIN2, the ancestor of the PLIN4-PLIN5-PLIN3 cluster, and plin6.
source: Phylogenetic analysis indicates that the vertebrate PLIN gene family arose by the duplication of a single gene present in a chordate ancestor (represented today by a gene in the urochordate Ciona (ENSCING00000004283)) in two rounds of whole genome duplication at the base of the vertebrate radiation giving four genes: PLIN1, PLIN2, the ancestor of the PLIN4-PLIN5-PLIN3 cluster, and plin6.
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic and synteny analyses presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: After the divergence of rayfin and lobefin vertebrates, plin6 went missing in the lobefin lineage but was retained in the rayfin lineage.
source: After the divergence of rayfin and lobefin vertebrates, plin6 went missing in the lobefin lineage but was retained in the rayfin lineage.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution of plin6 shown in Figure 1.

claim: In the lobefin lineage, one of the PLIN genes experienced a tandem duplication in the tetrapod lineage after it diverged from the coelacanth lineage producing PLIN3 and PLIN5.
source: In the lobefin lineage, one of the PLIN genes experienced a tandem duplication in the tetrapod lineage after it diverged from the coelacanth lineage producing PLIN3 and PLIN5.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution and genomic organization of PLIN3 and PLIN5.

claim: After the divergence of sauropsids from synapsids, PLIN5 underwent a tandem duplication, leaving PLIN5 and PLIN4.
source: Subsequently, after the divergence of sauropsids (birds and 'reptiles') from synapsids (mammals and mammal-like 'reptiles'), PLIN5 underwent a tandem duplication, leaving PLIN5 and PLIN4, completing the five-gene repertoire of the human PLIN family.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution of PLIN4 and PLIN5.

claim: After the teleost genome duplication, the four plin-family genes became eight genes that then reverted to single copy except for plin2.
source: Meanwhile, in the rayfin lineage, after the teleost genome duplication, the four plin-family genes became eight genes that then reverted to single copy except for plin2, which some percomorphs maintained as plin2a and plin2b.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution of plin genes in teleosts shown in Figure 1.

claim: Some percomorphs maintained plin2 as plin2a and plin2b.
source: Meanwhile, in the rayfin lineage, after the teleost genome duplication, the four plin-family genes became eight genes that then reverted to single copy except for plin2, which some percomorphs maintained as plin2a and plin2b.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic and synteny analyses shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Zebrafish have four plin genes, one copy of each of the original four that resulted after the vertebrate genome duplication events.
source: This process left the zebrafish with four plin genes, one copy of each of the original four that resulted after the vertebrate genome duplication events.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: These observations point to an ancient function of Plin6 in fish that was lost in tetrapod descendants.
source: These observations point to an ancient function of Plin6 in fish that was lost in tetrapod descendants.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution and functional data on Plin6.

claim: The conservation of the amphipathic N-terminal PAT domain suggested that Plin6 would likely be targeted to LD or LD-like structures.
source: The conservation of the amphipathic N-terminal PAT domain suggested that Plin6 would likely be targeted to LD or LD-like structures, yet its function might be unrelated to TAG storage and mobilization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known function of the PAT domain in other PLIN proteins.

claim: The function of Plin6 might be unrelated to TAG storage and mobilization.
source: The conservation of the amphipathic N-terminal PAT domain suggested that Plin6 would likely be targeted to LD or LD-like structures, yet its function might be unrelated to TAG storage and mobilization.
evidence: This is speculation based on the expression pattern of plin6 in skin rather than adipose tissue.

claim: The placement of PKA sites near the C-terminus in Plin6 is reminiscent of the PKA sites in mammalian PLIN1 that are critical for controlling its interactions with lipases and lipase activators.
source: Furthermore, the C-terminal region of Plin6 contains highly conserved consensus sites for phosphorylation by PKA. The placement of these PKA sites near the C-terminus is reminiscent of the PKA sites in mammalian PLIN1 that are critical for controlling its interactions with lipases and lipase activators (Subramanian et al., 2004; Marcinkiewicz et al., 2006; Miyoshi et al., 2007; Granneman et al., 2009); however, the regulatory sequences of PLIN1 likely evolved independently, because no significant amino acid similarity exists between the mammalian and teleost proteins in this region and in addition, PKA sites in Plin1 are not well conserved among lobefin descendants.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on PLIN1 function.

claim: The regulatory sequences of PLIN1 likely evolved independently from Plin6.
source: Furthermore, the C-terminal region of Plin6 contains highly conserved consensus sites for phosphorylation by PKA. The placement of these PKA sites near the C-terminus is reminiscent of the PKA sites in mammalian PLIN1 that are critical for controlling its interactions with lipases and lipase activators (Subramanian et al., 2004; Marcinkiewicz et al., 2006; Miyoshi et al., 2007; Granneman et al., 2009); however, the regulatory sequences of PLIN1 likely evolved independently, because no significant amino acid similarity exists between the mammalian and teleost proteins in this region and in addition, PKA sites in Plin1 are not well conserved among lobefin descendants.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of sequence similarity between PLIN1 and Plin6 in the C-terminal region.

claim: No significant amino acid similarity exists between mammalian PLIN1 and teleost Plin6 in the C-terminal region.
source: Furthermore, the C-terminal region of Plin6 contains highly conserved consensus sites for phosphorylation by PKA. The placement of these PKA sites near the C-terminus is reminiscent of the PKA sites in mammalian PLIN1 that are critical for controlling its interactions with lipases and lipase activators (Subramanian et al., 2004; Marcinkiewicz et al., 2006; Miyoshi et al., 2007; Granneman et al., 2009); however, the regulatory sequences of PLIN1 likely evolved independently, because no significant amino acid similarity exists between the mammalian and teleost proteins in this region and in addition, PKA sites in Plin1 are not well conserved among lobefin descendants.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: PKA sites in Plin1 are not well conserved among lobefin descendants.
source: Furthermore, the C-terminal region of Plin6 contains highly conserved consensus sites for phosphorylation by PKA. The placement of these PKA sites near the C-terminus is reminiscent of the PKA sites in mammalian PLIN1 that are critical for controlling its interactions with lipases and lipase activators (Subramanian et al., 2004; Marcinkiewicz et al., 2006; Miyoshi et al., 2007; Granneman et al., 2009); however, the regulatory sequences of PLIN1 likely evolved independently, because no significant amino acid similarity exists between the mammalian and teleost proteins in this region and in addition, PKA sites in Plin1 are not well conserved among lobefin descendants.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Plin6 mediates conserved functions that are specific to certain teleosts and likely involve PKA modulation of hydrophobic cargo trafficking.
source: Together, these results indicate that Plin6 mediates conserved functions that are specific to certain teleosts and likely involve PKA modulation of hydrophobic cargo trafficking.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of PKA sites and the functional data on CD trafficking.

claim: Carotenoid-based pigmentation is involved in several adaptive functions, such as cryptic coloration, conspecific recognition, and sexual selection.
source: We found that Plin6 is highly expressed in xanthophores and is specifically targeted to CD, which are involved several adaptive functions, such as cryptic coloration, conspecific recognition, and sexual selection (Price et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Carotenoid-based pigmentation is found in both vertebrates and invertebrates.
source: Carotenoid-based pigmentation is found in both vertebrates (Cote et al., 2010; Walsh et al., 2012) and invertebrates (Yang et al., 1999; Messenger, 2001), and substantial evidence indicates that CD and LD are homologous structures with a shared evolutionary history.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Substantial evidence indicates that CD and LD are homologous structures with a shared evolutionary history.
source: Carotenoid-based pigmentation is found in both vertebrates (Cote et al., 2010; Walsh et al., 2012) and invertebrates (Yang et al., 1999; Messenger, 2001), and substantial evidence indicates that CD and LD are homologous structures with a shared evolutionary history.
evidence: This is supported by the functional and structural data presented in the manuscript, including the ability of Plin6 to target mammalian LD.

claim: Fish CD were once referred to as 'lipophores' to emphasize the lipid content of these intracellular organelles.
source: Indeed, fish CD were once referred to as 'lipophores' to emphasize the lipid content of these intracellular organelles (Bagnara, 1966).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Ultrastructural investigations demonstrated that CD, like LD, contain a hydrophobic core surrounded by a phospholipid monolayer.
source: Furthermore, ultrastructural investigations by Taylor and colleagues (Kimler et al., 1993) demonstrated that CD, like LD, contain a hydrophobic core surrounded by a phospholipid monolayer.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Teleost CD are thought to be a constitutive subdomain of the SER.
source: Teleost CD are thought to be a constitutive subdomain of the SER (Kimler et al., 1993), whereas mammalian and yeast LD are thought to form in a specialized SER subdomain that is then released as independent LD (Goodman, 2009; Brasaemle and Wolins, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Mammalian and yeast LD are thought to form in a specialized SER subdomain that is then released as independent LD.
source: Teleost CD are thought to be a constitutive subdomain of the SER (Kimler et al., 1993), whereas mammalian and yeast LD are thought to form in a specialized SER subdomain that is then released as independent LD (Goodman, 2009; Brasaemle and Wolins, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mammalian LD that concentrate carotenoids (specifically retinylesters) contain PLIN proteins.
source: Mammalian LD that concentrate carotenoids (specifically retinylesters) contain PLIN proteins (Higashi and Senoo, 2003; Straub et al., 2008; Orban et al., 2011), and we show that zebrafish Plin6 and mouse PLIN1 target the same LD structures in mammalian cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Zebrafish Plin6 and mouse PLIN1 target the same LD structures in mammalian cells.
source: Mammalian LD that concentrate carotenoids (specifically retinylesters) contain PLIN proteins (Higashi and Senoo, 2003; Straub et al., 2008; Orban et al., 2011), and we show that zebrafish Plin6 and mouse PLIN1 target the same LD structures in mammalian cells.
evidence: Figure 8 shows co-localization of zebrafish Plin6 and mouse PLIN1 on lipid droplets in COS7 cells.

claim: Mammalian PLIN paralogs and splice variants can differentially concentrate cholesterol ester versus triglyceride within LD structures.
source: It has been previously shown that mammalian PLIN paralogs and splice variants can differentially concentrate cholesterol ester versus triglyceride within LD structures (Hsieh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The mechanisms involved in selective sequestration of hydrophobic cargo are not understood.
source: The mechanisms involved in selective sequestration of hydrophobic cargo are not understood, but could involve cell-specific transport, PLIN-interacting proteins, and the composition of the LD/CD phospholipid monolayer.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Selective sequestration of hydrophobic cargo could involve cell-specific transport, PLIN-interacting proteins, and the composition of the LD/CD phospholipid monolayer.
source: The mechanisms involved in selective sequestration of hydrophobic cargo are not understood, but could involve cell-specific transport, PLIN-interacting proteins, and the composition of the LD/CD phospholipid monolayer.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms.

claim: Mechanisms for concentrating carotenoid pigments are found widely in vertebrates and invertebrates.
source: The functional evolution of PLIN6 is somewhat a matter of speculation. Mechanisms for concentrating carotenoid pigments are found widely in vertebrates and invertebrates (Jouni and Wells, 1993; Tabunoki et al., 2004), and thus likely predate the appearance of bony fish.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mechanisms for concentrating carotenoid pigments likely predate the appearance of bony fish.
source: The functional evolution of PLIN6 is somewhat a matter of speculation. Mechanisms for concentrating carotenoid pigments are found widely in vertebrates and invertebrates (Jouni and Wells, 1993; Tabunoki et al., 2004), and thus likely predate the appearance of bony fish.
evidence: This is inferred from the widespread distribution of carotenoid concentration mechanisms.

claim: Fish obtain carotenoids only from their diet.
source: Because fish obtain carotenoids only from their diet, the pigmentation carotenoids confer is thought to represent an 'honest' index of foraging ability (Lindström et al., 2009; Pike et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about carotenoid acquisition in fish.

claim: The pigmentation carotenoids confer is thought to represent an 'honest' index of foraging ability.
source: Because fish obtain carotenoids only from their diet, the pigmentation carotenoids confer is thought to represent an 'honest' index of foraging ability (Lindström et al., 2009; Pike et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The antioxidant effects of carotenoids have been linked to increased male fertility in stickleback fish.
source: In addition, the antioxidant effects of carotenoids have been linked to increased male fertility in stickleback fish (Pike et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Expression of Plin6 increases the ability of xanthophores to concentrate pigment.
source: Our knockout data demonstrate that expression of Plin6 increases the ability of xanthophores to concentrate pigment, and thus could intensify a preexisting signal for sexual selection.
evidence: Figure 6 shows reduced carotenoid concentration in plin6 knockout fish.

claim: Plin6 could intensify a preexisting signal for sexual selection.
source: Our knockout data demonstrate that expression of Plin6 increases the ability of xanthophores to concentrate pigment, and thus could intensify a preexisting signal for sexual selection.
evidence: This is speculation based on the role of carotenoid pigmentation in sexual selection.

claim: Dynamic trafficking of melanosomes is found in several cell types and may be important in cryptic coloration.
source: Dynamic trafficking of melanosomes is found in several cell types and may be important in cryptic coloration (Bagnara and Hadley, 1969; Price et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Melanosomes and xanthophores derive from a common neural crest progenitor.
source: Because melanosomes and xanthophores derive from a common neural crest progenitor (Parichy and Spiewak, 2015), it seems likely that the basic machinery for PKA-induced trafficking predates evolution the of PKA phosphorylation sites in Plin6.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The basic machinery for PKA-induced trafficking likely predates evolution of the PKA phosphorylation sites in Plin6.
source: Because melanosomes and xanthophores derive from a common neural crest progenitor (Parichy and Spiewak, 2015), it seems likely that the basic machinery for PKA-induced trafficking predates evolution the of PKA phosphorylation sites in Plin6.
evidence: This is inferred from the shared developmental origin of melanosomes and xanthophores.

claim: With the possible exception of certain amphibians, lobefins lack either xanthophores in their entirety or the ability to aggregate and disperse CDs.
source: With the possible exception of certain amphibians, lobefins (sarcopterygians) lack either xanthophores in their entirety or the ability to aggregate and disperse CDs (Bagnara and Hadley, 1969).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The aggregation and dispersion of CDs across species is correlated with the presence of Plin6.
source: Therefore, the aggregation and dispersion of CDs across species is correlated with the presence of Plin6.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution of plin6 and the presence/absence of CD aggregation/dispersion.

claim: The function of Plin6 in CD trafficking would be lost in vertebrates lacking scales and/or carotenoid-based skin pigmentation.
source: Clearly, the function of Plin6 in CD trafficking would be lost in vertebrates lacking scales and/or carotenoid-based skin pigmentation.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the function of Plin6.

claim: Mammals lack both xanthophores and Plin6.
source: In this regard, mammals lack both xanthophores (Parichy and Spiewak, 2015) and, as we show here, Plin6.
evidence: The absence of xanthophores is supported by a citation, and the absence of Plin6 is shown in Figure 1.

claim: A common feature of all PLIN proteins is the ability to target structures with hydrophobic cargo surrounded by a phospholipid monolayer.
source: Finally, our results clearly indicate that CD and LD are homologous structures. A common feature of all PLIN proteins is the ability to target structures with hydrophobic cargo surrounded by a phospholipid monolayer.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PLIN protein function.

claim: Diversification and specialization of Plin paralogs throughout evolution seem to have been driven by cell-specific expression and interactions with specific binding partners.
source: Diversification and specialization of Plin paralogs throughout evolution seem to have been driven by cell-specific expression and interactions with specific binding partners (Granneman et al., 2007, 2009, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Plin6 has unique properties, including selective expression in xanthophores, the ability to influence the organization of CD, the ability to concentrate specific cargo, and the potential to interact with trafficking machinery.
source: In this regard, Plin6 appears to have unique properties, including selective expression in xanthophores, the ability to influence the organization of CD, the ability to concentrate specific cargo, and the potential to interact with trafficking machinery.
evidence: These properties are demonstrated by the expression, localization, and functional data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Further analysis of Plin6 will inform our understanding of LD, PLIN protein biology, and the evolutionary mechanisms giving rise to the wonderful color variations that are so important for the biology of teleost fish.
source: We anticipate that further analysis of Plin6 will inform our understanding of LD, PLIN protein biology, and the evolutionary mechanisms giving rise to the wonderful color variations that are so important for the biology of teleost fish, half of all vertebrate species.
evidence: This is speculation about the future impact of this research.

claim: Teleost fish represent half of all vertebrate species.
source: We anticipate that further analysis of Plin6 will inform our understanding of LD, PLIN protein biology, and the evolutionary mechanisms giving rise to the wonderful color variations that are so important for the biology of teleost fish, half of all vertebrate species.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the diversity of teleost fish.
